rules.K1: The scarf is knitted from the first chapter to the last. Every passage of the book is one pair of rows: a right-side row and the row back.
rules.K2: The reader labels every sentence warm, cold or neither, and does so twice, with the question put in different words. For a passage, take the warm labels minus the cold ones over both readings and divide by the number of labels. Yarn A if that is -0.5 or less, B if below -0.2, C if below 0.2, D if below 0.5, E otherwise.
rules.K3: In both readings the reader also labels every sentence tense or calm. If at least 50 in 100 of a passage's labels are tense, the row back is knitted, which leaves a raised ridge you can feel; otherwise it is purled and the fabric is smooth. Three stitches at each edge are always knitted so the scarf lies flat.
rules.K4: The 10 most-mentioned people each own a column. The most-mentioned is in the middle and the others alternate outwards. A person is someone the reader named, or a description the book itself uses as a name at least three times: one written with a capital (the Ghost), or a named person's relation (Scrooge's nephew).
rules.K5: On the right-side row a person's column gets an eyelet (yarn over, knit two together) if the reader has a verified fact that they are in that passage. Otherwise the column is knitted plain.
rules.K6: The first passage of every chapter has an eyelet in the edge, so chapters can be counted along one side.
rules.K7: The two readings are also counted apart. If on their own they would pick yarns two or more apart (A and C, say), the passage is knitted in undyed yarn U: the answer depends too much on how the question was put, so the scarf makes no claim.

gauge.note: Typical figures for worsted yarn; sizes and yardage are estimates until you swatch.

palette.name: Violet and marmalade
palette.from: a dream colour, and the jar Alice takes as she falls
palette.note: The colours are a choice, not a count: no book names colours often enough to count them. In every palette cold is the cool colour and warm the warm one, and undyed is cream.

rules.K2: One yarn. The reader labels every sentence warm, cold or neither, twice, and the count picks a class exactly as in the coloured scarf: A if the balance is -0.5 or less, B if below -0.2, C if below 0.2, D if below 0.5, E otherwise. The class says how much of the right-side row is purled: A all of it, B three stitches in four, C every other stitch, D one in four, E none. So a cold passage is rough under the hand and a warm one is smooth. On the row back, work each stitch as it faces you (knit the knits, purl the purls). The purls shift along on every other passage, so the scarf does not pull in like ribbing.
rules.K3: Two knit stitches near one edge make a rope, with a purl stitch on each side of it. If at least 50 in 100 of a passage's labels are tense, cross the two (a right twist) on the right-side row; otherwise knit them straight. So the rope twists where the book is tense. Three stitches at each edge are always knitted so the scarf lies flat.
rules.K7: The two readings are also counted apart. If on their own they would pick classes two or more apart (A and C, say), both rows of the passage are knitted plain, which leaves one flat ridge with no pattern in it: the scarf makes no claim.

abbreviations.RT: right twist: knit the second stitch on the left needle without slipping it off, then knit the first, and slip both off together

yarn.name: one light, smooth yarn
yarn.note: Texture shows best in a light, plain yarn; a dark or fuzzy one hides it.
